title: The milkmaid's vocation
hookLine: Luther said a milkmaid's work pleases God as much as a monk's

lines: A STOOL IN A COLD BARN.
cards: Before dawn, in a cold barn, a young woman sits on a stool with her cheek against a cow's warm side, and the milk rings into the pail. Up the hill, in a monastery, a monk is already at prayer in the chapel.
Ask the village which of the two is doing holy work, and the answer comes fast. Martin Luther gave a different answer, and it startled people.
Christians still repeat a saying credited to him: the milkmaid's work, done in faith, pleases God as much as the monk's.

teach.b: A vocation is a calling. In the world Luther grew up in, the word had come to belong to one kind of life: priests, monks and nuns. They had a calling; everyone else simply had a job.
He argued that God calls the farmer, the parent, the shoemaker and the servant girl just as truly, and that their work serves God by serving neighbors. The baby gets fed. The town has shoes.
The bread arrives. He leaned on Paul's advice to the Corinthians: "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called." Your ordinary station is where faith gets lived.

teach.h: DO IT HEARTILY, AS TO THE LORD.
teach.b: Paul says it another way in Colossians, writing to people who were servants: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Notice who that was written to. Not preachers.
This idea took root in the churches that came from Luther, and it isn't only theirs: Catholic teaching today also speaks of the vocation of lay people, and of work as a share in God's own work.
Luther, a former monk himself, never stopped praying. What he argued against was the idea that a monk's vows earned more with God than a farmer's faith.
He refused a ladder, with spiritual jobs at the top and the barn at the bottom. Diapers, spreadsheets, a cash register: in this view, they can be a calling too.

how: Lutheran and other Protestant churches teach the doctrine of vocation, that ordinary work and family life are callings from God; Catholic teaching also speaks of the vocation of lay people in the world, and some churches bless workers and their tools.

o: a strong talent you were simply born with
training for a trade, like a plumber's
a calling from God, in any honest work

games.q: the milkmaid's calling — tap the pairs.
p: do it heartily, as to the Lord

s: Luther thought only clergy had a real calling
the opposite: he taught that God calls the farmer, the parent and the servant girl as truly as the monk.
Paul is writing to servants: their work, done heartily, is done for the Lord.
Catholic teaching also speaks of a vocation for lay people
it speaks of the vocation of lay people and of work as a share in God's work.

games.q: you're the milkmaid. a traveling preacher tells you the monk's prayers please God more than your milking. what does Luther say?
o: he's right; leave the barn for the convent.
your work, done in faith, pleases God too.
only the work done on Sunday counts.
games.why: Luther refused the ladder of holy jobs. the barn can be a calling as much as the chapel, because the work serves a neighbor.

practice: Bring to mind the most ordinary task waiting for you today, the email, the dishes, the shift, and trace it outward until you can picture one actual person on the other end. Then picture doing that task heartily, for them.
If you pray, you can offer it to God before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Vocation. A calling. In Luther's teaching, not only for priests and monks, but for anyone whose ordinary work serves a neighbor.

orig.note: Greek, 1 Corinthians 7:20: a calling, the word Paul uses for where a person was called.

carryVoice: Your line: every job is holy. The barn and the chapel, both. Back tomorrow, same hill.
